## Assessing Heat Vulnerability and Chronic Condition Prevalence in NYC: An Exploratory Analysis

Overview: This project explores the potential relationship between heat vulnerability and chronic condition prevalence in the New York City (NYC) area. The data come from the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (NYC DOHMH) website and are publicly available for download. In addition to exploring relationships between heat vulnerability and chronic condition prevalence, this project also seeks to identify potential community-level disparities that warrant further consideration.

## Introduction:

Heat exposure is a leading cause of weather-related deaths in the United States \[1\]. Heat exposure is also quite common; more than two-thirds of Americans were under heat alerts in 2023 \[2\]. Extreme heat is a particularly serious environmental health risk to New York City (NYC) residents. In fact, extreme heat is NYC's deadliest weather hazard, taking more lives than hurricanes, floods, or winter storms \[3\]. Between 2018 and 2022, there were an average of 525 heat-related deaths per year in NYC \[3\]. Most of these deaths occur in New Yorkers’ own homes, often without air conditioning (AC) \[3\]. The risk is greatest among communities already impacted by housing inequities, which disproportionately affects black New Yorkers \[3\].

Approximately 100 heat-exacerbated deaths each year are attributable to the most extreme heat days \[3\]. Extreme heat days are defined as days that meet the extreme heat advisory threshold in NYC from the National Weather Service \[3\]. The remaining heat-exacerbated deaths occurred on non-extreme heat days, days below the heat advisory threshold but above 82 degrees Fahrenheit \[3\]. Although these are not considered extreme weather days, they remain dangerous; the number of these types of days has increased more rapidly over the past decade than extreme heat days \[3\]. Further, although non-extreme heat days have increased rapidly, home AC rates have remained steady, suggesting AC access is not keeping pace with rising demand \[3\]. This is dangerous because without AC, indoor temperatures can become much hotter than outdoor temperatures, especially at night, and can persist for days following a heat wave \[3\].

Higher temperatures pose especially serious risks in NYC, where extreme heat can exacerbate the urban heat island effect \[4\]. Buildings, roads, and other infrastructure absorb and re-emit heat more than natural landscapes such as forests and bodies of water; as a result, urban areas become “islands” of higher temperatures relative to outlying areas \[5\].

While heat exposure is clearly associated with a higher risk of heat exhaustion and heat stroke \[6\], it also exacerbates multiple chronic conditions \[7\]. People with chronic conditions may be more vulnerable to heat because they have a reduced ability to sense and respond to temperature changes and may take medications that worsen heat effects \[7\]. Further, warmer weather traps greenhouse gases in the atmosphere and worsens ozone levels, which can irritate lung tissue \[8\]. High ozone levels or long-term exposure can worsen respiratory symptoms and conditions, including asthma \[8\].

Similarly, extreme heat events often exacerbate diabetes-related complications \[9\]. Diabetes can damage blood vessels and nerves, reducing the body’s ability to cool itself effectively \[9\]. Further, people with diabetes dehydrate more quickly, which is associated with raised blood sugar, and high temperatures can change the way that the body uses insulin \[9\].

Lastly, high temperatures and high humidity, in particular, affect people managing hypertension. When exposed to high temperatures, the body redirects blood flow to the skin to cool itself, which can raise blood pressure and increase heart rate; dehydration from sweating also reduces blood volume, further stressing the heart and potentially raising blood pressure \[10\]. The combination of these two mechanisms can exacerbate existing hypertension and put people at an increased risk of experiencing heart failure, arrhythmias, or acute cardiac events \[10\].

Using a health equity lens, this assessment will use epidemiologic methods to characterize and analyze the relationship between heat vulnerability, geography, and the prevalence of chronic conditions in NYC.

## Methods + Results

## Part 1: Initial Correlations + Regression Model

Step 1: Download and Install Packages

```{r}
library(tidyverse) 
library(sf) 
library(tidycensus) 
library(janitor)
library(tmap) 
library(dplyr) 
library(readr)
```

Step 2: Load ZIP code geography

```{r}

zip_shapes <- st_read("C:/Users/alyss/Downloads/Modified_Zip_Code_Tabulation_Areas_(MODZCTA)_20260605.geojson")

```

Step 3: Load Heat Vulnerability Index (HVI)

```{r}

hvi <- read_csv("C:/Users/alyss/Downloads/Heat_Vulnerability_Index_Rankings_20260605.csv")

clean_names(hvi)

```

Step 4: Load Chronic Condition Data

```{r}

NEWasthma <- read_csv("C:/Users/alyss/Downloads/NEW Asthma Dataset.xlsx - Sheet1.csv")
NEWdiabetes <- read_csv("C:/Users/alyss/Downloads/NEW Diabetes Dataset.xlsx - Sheet1.csv")
NEWhypertension <- read_csv("C:/Users/alyss/Downloads/NEW Hypertension Dataset.xlsx - Sheet1.csv")

```

Step 5: Merge chronic condition data

```{r}

chroncondition_data1 <- NEWasthma %>%
  left_join(NEWdiabetes, by = "Zip Code") %>%
  left_join(NEWhypertension, by= "Zip Code")


```

Step 6: Merge with HVI data

```{r}

hvi <- read_csv("C:/Users/alyss/Downloads/Heat_Vulnerability_Index_Rankings_20260605.csv") %>%
  clean_names()

hvi <- hvi %>%
  rename(zip_code = zip_code_tabulation_area_zcta_2020)

NEWasthma <- NEWasthma %>% clean_names()
NEWdiabetes <- NEWdiabetes %>% clean_names()
NEWhypertension <- NEWhypertension %>% clean_names()

chroncondition_data1 <- NEWasthma %>%
  left_join(NEWdiabetes, by = "zip_code") %>%
  left_join(NEWhypertension, by = "zip_code")

hvi <- read_csv("C:/Users/alyss/Downloads/Heat_Vulnerability_Index_Rankings_20260605.csv") %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  rename(zip_code = zip_code_tabulation_area_zcta_2020)

chroncondition_data1 <- chroncondition_data1 %>%
  mutate(zip_code = as.character(zip_code))

hvi <- hvi %>%
  mutate(zip_code = as.character(zip_code))


NEWanalysis_data <- chroncondition_data1 %>%
  left_join(hvi, by = "zip_code")


```

Step 7: check class

```{r}

class(NEWanalysis_data$estimated_prevalence.y)
class(NEWanalysis_data$heat_vulnerability_index_hvi)

```

Step 8: Run correlations

```{r}

## HVI score v. asthma prevalence

cor.test(NEWanalysis_data$heat_vulnerability_index_hvi, NEWanalysis_data$estimated_prevalence.x)

## t-value= 2.4115
## p-value= 0.0218 (statistically significant)
## 95% CI: 0.062-0.645
## cor= 0.392 (weak/moderate linear relationship)

## HVI score v. diabetes prevalence

cor.test(NEWanalysis_data$heat_vulnerability_index_hvi, NEWanalysis_data$estimated_prevalence.y)

## t-value= 2.865
## p-value= 0.000511 (very statistically significant)
## 95% CI: 0.279-0.758
## cor= 0.564 (moderate linear relationship)

## HVI score v. hypertension prevalence

cor.test(NEWanalysis_data$heat_vulnerability_index_hvi, NEWanalysis_data$estimated_prevalence)

## t-value= 2.9141
## p-value= 0.006461 (very statistically significant)
## 95% CI: 0.142-0.689
## cor= 0.457 (moderate linear relationship)

```

Step 9: Run SLR

CAVEAT: Only moderate linear relationships identified between HVI and these 3 chronic conditions, so interpret cautiously

```{r}

SLRmodel <- lm(NEWanalysis_data$heat_vulnerability_index_hvi ~ NEWanalysis_data$estimated_prevalence.x + NEWanalysis_data$estimated_prevalence.y + NEWanalysis_data$estimated_prevalence)
summary(SLRmodel)
```

Under an SLR, none of the chronic conditions' prevalence were significantly associated with HVI; however, asthma is borderline significant. Weaker linear relationships between diabetes and heat vulnerability and hypertension and heat vulnerability may be influencing these results

Findings: Weak-to-moderate correlations between HVI and chronic conditions and non-significant regression coefficients

Interpretation: Chronic condition prevalence ALONE does not strongly track with HVI at the ZIP level. This makes sense because HVI includes many components, including housing quality, access to AC, green space, poverty, etc. Chronic disease is just one piece of vulnerability.

## Part 2: Re-framing as a Stratified Analysis

Step 1: Stratify ZIP codes by HVI

```{r}

NEWanalysis_data <- NEWanalysis_data %>%
  mutate(hvi_group= ntile(heat_vulnerability_index_hvi, 4)) 

# quartiles

```

Step 2: Compare chronic disease across groups

```{r}

NEWanalysis_data %>%
  group_by(hvi_group) %>%
  summarise(
    asthma= mean(estimated_prevalence.x, na.rm= TRUE),
    diabetes= mean(estimated_prevalence.y, na.rm= TRUE),
    htn= mean(estimated_prevalence, na.rm= TRUE)
  )

```

Output: Residents in the highest HVI quartile have a 6% higher asthma prevalence compared to those in the lowest quartile. Residents in the highest HVI quartile have an 8% higher diabetes prevalence compared to those in the lowest quartile. Residents in the highest HVI quartile have a 10% higher hypertension prevalence compared to those in the lowest quartile.

Step 3: Show concentration of chronic condition prevalence by zip code

```{r}

my_tibble <- NEWanalysis_data %>%
  arrange(desc(heat_vulnerability_index_hvi)) %>%
  mutate(cum_pop= row_number()/n(),
         cum_hvi= cumsum(heat_vulnerability_index_hvi)/sum(heat_vulnerability_index_hvi))

print(my_tibble, n= Inf, width= Inf)

```

## Part 3: Create a composite chronic disease burden score

Step 1: Standardize each condition

```{r}

NEWanalysis_data <- NEWanalysis_data %>%
  mutate(
    asthma_z = as.numeric(scale(estimated_prevalence.x)),
    diabetes_z= as.numeric(scale(estimated_prevalence.y)),
    hypertension_z= as.numeric(scale(estimated_prevalence))
  )

```

Step 2: Create Composite Burden Score

```{r}

NEWanalysis_data <- NEWanalysis_data %>%
  mutate(
    burden_score=
      asthma_z +
      diabetes_z +
      hypertension_z
  )

```

Check first few rows

```{r}

head(
  NEWanalysis_data %>%
    select(
      zip_code,
      estimated_prevalence.x,
      estimated_prevalence.y,
      estimated_prevalence,
      burden_score
    )
)

```

Step 3: Correlation between burden score and HVI

```{r}

cor.test(
  NEWanalysis_data$heat_vulnerability_index_hvi,
  NEWanalysis_data$burden_score,
  method= "spearman"
)

```

A spearman correlation analysis was conducted to assess the association between HVI and a composite chronic condition burden score derived from asthma, diabetes, and hypertension prevalence.

Step 4: New Regression Analysis

```{r}

burden_model <- lm(
  burden_score ~ heat_vulnerability_index_hvi,
  data= NEWanalysis_data
)

summary(burden_model)

```

Here, HVI is significantly associated with the burden score. ZIP codes with higher HVI scores do tend to have higher composite chronic disease burden scores.

Step 5: Create Figure

```{r}

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(NEWanalysis_data,
       aes(
         x= heat_vulnerability_index_hvi,
         y= burden_score
       )
       )+
  geom_jitter(
    width= 0.1,
    alpha= 0.6,
    color= "steelblue"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method= "lm",
    color= "red",
    se= TRUE
  ) +
  labs(
    title= "Association Between Heat Vulnerability and Chronic Disease Burden",
    x= "Heat Vulnerability Index",
    y= "Composite Disease Burden Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

## Part 4: Identify neighborhoods with both high heat vulnerability and high chronic disease burden

Step 1: Define high disease burden

Top quartile of highest chronic disease burden

```{r}

burden_cutoff <- quantile(
  NEWanalysis_data$burden_score,
  probs= 0.75,
  na.rm= TRUE
)

```

Step 2: Create high-risk indicators

```{r}

NEWanalysis_data <- NEWanalysis_data %>%
  mutate(
    high_hvi=
      ifelse(
        heat_vulnerability_index_hvi >= 4,
        1,
        0
      ),
    high_burden= 
      ifelse(
        burden_score >= burden_cutoff,
        1,
        0
      )
  )

```

Step 3: Create risk categories

```{r}

NEWanalysis_data <- NEWanalysis_data %>%
  mutate(
    risk_group= case_when(
      high_hvi == 1 &
        high_burden == 1 ~
        "High HVI + High Chronic Condition Burden",
      high_hvi == 1 &
        high_burden == 0 ~
        "High HVI Only",
      high_hvi == 0 &
        high_burden == 1 ~
        "High Disease Only",
      TRUE ~
        "Neither"
    )
  )

```

Step 4: Examine Counts

```{r}

NEWanalysis_data %>%
  count(risk_group)
```

High Disease Only: 2

High HVI + High Chronic Condition: 7

High HVI Only: 12

Neither: 13

Step 5: Identify priority ZIP codes

```{r}

priority_zips <- NEWanalysis_data %>%
  filter(
    risk_group ==
      "High HVI + High Disease"
  ) %>%
  select(
    zip_code,
    heat_vulnerability_index_hvi,
    burden_score,
    estimated_prevalence.x,
    estimated_prevalence.y,
    estimated_prevalence
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(burden_score))

priority_zips

```

Step 7: Mapping

Merge spatial data

```{r}

names(zip_shapes)

```

Get the map- map composite burden score

```{r}

zip_shapes <- zip_shapes %>%
  mutate(modzcta = as.character(modzcta))

map_data <- zip_shapes %>%
  left_join(
    NEWanalysis_data,
    by= c("modzcta"= "zip_code")
  )

tm_shape(map_data) +
  tm_fill(
    col = "burden_score",
    palette = "RdYlBu",
    style = "quantile",
    title = "Disease Burden"
  ) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(
    title = "Composite Chronic Disease Burden"
  )
```

Mapping combined risk categories

```{r}

tm_shape(map_data) +
  tm_fill(
    col = "risk_group",
    palette = c(
      "red",
      "orange",
      "gold",
      "lightgrey"
    ),
    title = "Risk Category"
  ) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(
    title = "Neighborhoods with High Heat Vulnerability and High Chronic Disease Burden"
  )

```

## Discussion

This exploratory analysis evaluated the relationship between neighborhood-level heat vulnerability and chronic condition burden across NYC ZIP codes. Initial analyses indicated weak to moderate positive, linear correlations between HVI and the presence of asthma, diabetes, and hypertension individually; however, the subsequent regression analyses demonstrated that no single condition could independently explain variation in heat vulnerability. These findings suggested that chronic condition prevalence alone does not fully explain the variety of factors included within the HVI, as this is a composite metric that includes environmental, housing, and socioeconomic characteristics in addition to health-related indicators.

When chronic conditions were considered collectively by creating a composite chronic condition burden score, a more tangible relationship emerged. The composite burden score was significantly associated with HVI, indicating that neighborhoods experiencing greater heat vulnerability may also be simultaneously experiencing multiple chronic conditions. This is important because it highlights the potential cumulative impact of chronic condition burden rather than the influence of any single chronic condition in isolation. Communities do not just experience health risks independently; rather, chronic conditions often cluster geographically within neighborhoods also experiencing economic disadvantage, limited access to AC, less access to tree coverage and green space, housing vulnerabilities, and other environmental and structural barriers. As a result, the composite burden analysis provides a broader perspective on population health vulnerability and may be a better representation of how health risks interact with communities in the context of heat vulnerability.

The geographic analyses completed further support this idea. Mapping of both HVI and the composite condition burden score indicated visible concentrations of vulnerability across specific ZIP codes. In addition, identifying neighborhoods with both high HVI and high chronic condition burden demonstrates that some communities are experiencing a “double burden” of risk. Consequently, these areas could be particularly vulnerable during periods of high to extreme heat because residents face the combined challenges of environmental exposure and underlying health conditions associated with increased susceptibility to negative health outcomes.

From a public health perspective, these findings have critical implications for environmental and climate adaptation planning. The HVI was specifically created to identify communities already at an increased risk for heat-related morbidity and mortality. Understanding that neighborhoods with higher HVI scores also tend to experience greater cumulative chronic condition burden suggests that environment-related risks may disproportionately affect communities already experiencing higher baseline health burdens. As extreme heat events become more frequent and severe, interventions such as cooling centers, targeted outreach, urban green space initiatives, and chronic condition management programs should be prioritized in neighborhoods already experiencing both increased heat vulnerability and chronic condition burden.

## Limitations

It is important to note that limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, this analysis was cross-sectional and relied on publicly available datasets from the NYC DOHMH. Because data were collected at a single point in time, causal relationships cannot be estimated. While potential associations between heat vulnerability and chronic condition burden were identified, it is not possible to determine the directionality of these relationships or whether unmeasured or confounding variables are contributing to the observed patterns.

Another limitation to note is that the analysis was conducted at the ZIP code level; as a result, ecological limitations should be acknowledged. Residents within the same ZIP code can experience wide variation in socioeconomic circumstances, environmental exposures, and health status that cannot be captured by using aggregated measures. Additionally, several ZIP codes contained missing data, which results in reduced geographic coverage and could limit the generalizability of findings.

Lastly, the HVI is itself a composite measure that incorporates several environmental and socioeconomic indicators. As a result, observed relationships between HVI and chronic condition burden may partially reflect underlying social and structural determinants of health rather than heat vulnerability alone. 

## Conclusions

This exploratory analysis examined the relationship between heat vulnerability and chronic condition prevalence at the neighborhood level across NYC ZIP codes. While asthma, diabetes, and hypertension were only modestly associated with heat vulnerability when evaluated individually, a composite chronic condition score demonstrated a stronger relationship with HVI, suggesting that cumulative health burden could be more informative than information on any single condition alone. Geographic analyses further identified neighborhoods experiencing both heat vulnerability and high chronic condition burden, highlighting areas particularly susceptible to negative health outcomes during extreme heat events. These findings support the need to consider both environmental and heat-related factors when assessing community vulnerability and allocating public health resources.
